title: Translators, Scholars and 1893
bigQuestion: How did translators, scholars and Asian Buddhist teachers bring Buddhist texts to English readers, and how did their choices shape what readers understood?

story.title: A Voice in White Robes
story.kicker: A young Sri Lankan speaker stands before a crowd in Chicago in September 1893.
paragraphs: In September 1893, Chicago was hosting the World's Columbian Exposition, a huge world's fair. Alongside it, in a new building on Michigan Avenue that later became the Art Institute, leaders of many religions gathered for the World's Parliament of Religions.

One speaker was Anagarika Dharmapala, a Buddhist from Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, who was not yet thirty. He wore white robes. He spoke in English about the Buddha's teaching. He told the audience that Buddhism valued reason, kindness and self-effort.

Another Buddhist speaker came from Japan: Soyen Shaku, a Rinzai Zen abbot. His talk was translated into English by a young man who would become famous himself, D.T. Suzuki. It was read to the crowd in English.

For many Americans in the hall, this was the first time they had heard Buddhists explain their own tradition in person. Newspapers reported the speeches. Some listeners began to read Buddhist books, many of them recent English translations.
story.think: Why might it matter that Buddhists spoke for themselves at the Parliament, rather than being described by others?

lessons.title: Max Müller and the Sacred Books of the East
lessons.mainIdea: Max Müller edited the Sacred Books of the East (1879–1910), 50 volumes of Asian scriptures in English.
reading: Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900) was a German-born scholar at Oxford University. He studied Sanskrit and the history of religions. He believed Western readers should be able to read the scriptures of Asia in English.

Müller planned and edited the *Sacred Books of the East*, a series of 50 volumes published by Oxford from 1879 to 1910. It included Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Chinese, Zoroastrian and Islamic texts. Müller himself translated the Dhammapada for volume 10 (1881).

The series made these texts widely available for the first time. Scholars today note that it also reflected its era: Müller chose which texts counted as 'sacred books' and treated religions as mainly about texts, not *practice*.

words.d: a 50-volume Oxford series of Asian scriptures in English (1879–1910), edited by Max Müller
what religious people do, such as rituals, festivals and daily habits

look.title: The Mind Comes First
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 1; tr. F. Max Müller, The Dhammapada, Sacred Books of the East 10 (1881)
look.prompt: What does this verse say comes first? How might an English reader in 1881 have reacted?

check.q: Who edited the Sacred Books of the East?
check.why: Müller planned and edited the series.

check.q: How many volumes did the series have?
check.why: The series ran to 50 volumes.

check.q: What criticism do scholars make of the series today?

It treated religions mainly as texts, not practice
check.why: The series focused on scripture and chose what counted as sacred.

lessons.title: T.W. and Caroline Rhys Davids
lessons.mainIdea: T.W. and Caroline Rhys Davids translated and published Pali texts through the Pali Text Society.
reading: T.W. Rhys Davids learned Pali from Buddhist monks while serving as a British official in Sri Lanka. He founded the Pali Text Society in 1881 and translated many suttas, including Buddhist Suttas (SBE 11, 1881).

His wife, *Caroline Rhys Davids* (1857–1942), was a scholar in her own right. She translated the Therigatha as *Psalms of the Sisters* (1909) and worked on the Abhidhamma. She later led the Pali Text Society as president.
Their work relied on Sri Lankan and Burmese monks, who taught them the language and supplied manuscripts. Historians today stress this *collaboration*, which older accounts often left out.

words.d: British scholar (1857–1942) who translated the Therigatha and led the Pali Text Society

look.title: A Family of Translators
look.cite: Pali Text Society history; standard bibliographies
look.prompt: How many years passed between the society's founding and Psalms of the Sisters?

check.q: Where did T.W. Rhys Davids learn Pali?
check.why: He learned from monks while in Sri Lanka.

check.q: What did Caroline Rhys Davids translate as Psalms of the Sisters?
check.why: She translated the nuns' verses in 1909.

check.q: Whose help do historians now stress in this work?
check.why: Asian monks taught the language and supplied manuscripts.

lessons.title: The Light of Asia
lessons.mainIdea: Edwin Arnold's poem The Light of Asia (1879) told the Buddha's life in English verse and became a bestseller.
reading: In 1879, the English poet Edwin Arnold published *The Light of Asia*, a long poem about the life of the Buddha. It retold the story from the prince's birth to his awakening and teaching.

The poem was hugely popular in Britain and America, selling hundreds of thousands of copies. For many readers, it was their first picture of the Buddha. Its language made the Buddha sound like a noble Victorian hero.

Arnold's poem also mattered in Asia. Anagarika Dharmapala later said reading it moved him deeply. Scholars note that a *poem* like this shapes an image of the Buddha that is partly the poet's own; it is a *retelling*, not a translation.

words.d: Edwin Arnold's 1879 poem about the life of the Buddha
telling a story again in new words, often with changes

look.title: Translation or Retelling?
look.text: A translator tries to carry a text's words into another language. A poet retelling a story adds images, feelings and ideas of their own. The Light of Asia draws on Buddhist biographies but is Arnold's own poem.
look.prompt: Why is it important to know whether you are reading a translation or a retelling?

check.q: Who wrote The Light of Asia?
check.why: Arnold published the poem in 1879.

check.q: What is The Light of Asia?
choices: A poem retelling the Buddha's life
check.why: It is an English verse retelling.

check.q: Why do scholars call it a retelling rather than a translation?
choices: The poet added his own images and ideas
check.why: A retelling is partly the author's own creation.

lessons.title: The World's Parliament of Religions
lessons.mainIdea: The 1893 Parliament in Chicago was the first large meeting where Asian religious leaders spoke to Americans in person.
reading: The *World's Parliament of Religions* met in Chicago from September 11 to 27, 1893, as part of the World's Columbian Exposition. It is often seen as the start of formal interfaith dialogue in the modern West.
Speakers included Christians and Jews as well as Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and others. The Hindu teacher Swami Vivekananda became famous for his opening words, 'Sisters and brothers of America'.

Some organizers hoped the Parliament would show Christianity as the highest religion. Asian speakers used the platform to present their own traditions on their own terms. Historians see it as a turning point in American knowledge of *world religions*, and of *interfaith* meeting.

words.d: a gathering of religious leaders in Chicago, September 1893
the major religious traditions studied across the globe

lessons.title: Anagarika Dharmapala
lessons.mainIdea: Dharmapala, a Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer, spoke at the Parliament and worked to restore Buddhist sites in India.
reading: *Anagarika Dharmapala* (1864–1933) was born in Colombo, Sri Lanka, then a British colony. He grew up during a Buddhist revival that resisted Christian missionary schools. 'Anagarika' means 'homeless one', a title he took as a layman devoted full-time to Buddhism.

In 1891 he founded the Maha Bodhi Society to restore Bodh Gaya, where Buddhists believe the Buddha reached awakening. At the 1893 Parliament, he presented Buddhism as rational and compatible with science.

Dharmapala returned to America several times and helped spread Buddhism abroad. Some historians call his approach *Buddhist modernism*: presenting Buddhism in terms of reason and ethics for modern audiences. Sri Lankans honor him as a national hero.

words.d: Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer (1864–1933) who spoke at the 1893 Parliament
presenting Buddhism in terms of reason, science and ethics for modern readers

look.title: Speaking to a New Audience
look.text: Dharmapala stood before a mostly Christian American crowd. He chose to stress reason, kindness and self-reliance. He said less about rebirth rituals, relics or temple offerings that were central to many Sri Lankan Buddhists' lives.
look.prompt: Why might he have chosen what to stress? What might listeners have missed?

check.q: Where was Dharmapala from?
check.why: He was born in Colombo, Sri Lanka.

check.q: What did the Maha Bodhi Society seek to restore?
check.why: Bodh Gaya is the place of the Buddha's awakening.

check.q: What is Buddhist modernism?
choices: Presenting Buddhism through reason and ethics for modern readers
check.why: Historians use the term for reformers like Dharmapala.

lessons.title: Soyen Shaku and D.T. Suzuki
lessons.mainIdea: Soyen Shaku spoke for Japanese Zen in 1893, and his student D.T. Suzuki later made Zen famous in the West.
reading: *Soyen Shaku* (1860–1919) was abbot of Engakuji, a Rinzai Zen temple in Kamakura, Japan. He spoke at the 1893 Parliament, with his speech translated into English by his lay student, D.T. Suzuki.

*D.T. Suzuki* (1870–1966) then came to America. From 1897 he lived for about eleven years in La Salle, Illinois, working for Paul Carus of the Open Court Publishing Company, translating Asian texts. Carus himself had written The Gospel of Buddha (1894).

Suzuki later wrote many English books on Zen. From the 1950s, his lectures at Columbia University influenced writers, artists and thinkers. Scholars today note that Suzuki presented Zen in his own way, sometimes stressing experience over ritual and monastic life.

words.d: Japanese Rinzai Zen abbot (1860–1919) who spoke at the 1893 Parliament
Japanese scholar (1870–1966) who wrote many English books on Zen

check.why: Suzuki, his student, translated it.

check.q: What do scholars note about how Suzuki presented Zen?
choices: He stressed experience over ritual and monastic life
check.why: His presentation shaped Western ideas of Zen.

lessons.title: Suffering or Unsatisfactoriness?
lessons.mainIdea: Translators render dukkha as 'suffering', 'pain', 'stress' or 'unsatisfactoriness', and each choice shapes the reader.
reading: The Pali word *dukkha* is at the center of the Four Noble Truths. Rhys Davids and most early translators put it as 'suffering' or 'pain'. That made Buddhism sound gloomy to some Western readers.

Later translators argued that dukkha covers more than pain: it includes the sense that things never fully satisfy because they change. Some chose 'unsatisfactoriness'; others use 'stress' or leave the word untranslated.

Each choice brings out one side of the idea. A reader who sees only 'suffering' might think Buddhism is pessimistic. A reader who sees 'unsatisfactoriness' might think it is about mild dissatisfaction. Scholars say careful readers learn the original word and its *connotation*, or feeling.

words.d: a Pali word translated as suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness (Sanskrit: duhkha)
the feelings and ideas a word suggests beyond its basic meaning

look.title: Three Translations of One Line
look.text: Translation A: 'Birth is suffering, old age is suffering.' Translation B: 'Birth is stressful, aging is stressful.' Translation C: 'Birth is unsatisfactory, aging is unsatisfactory.' All three render the same Pali line of Samyutta Nikaya 56.11.
look.prompt: How does each translation make you feel? Which do you think is closest to the idea taught in this unit?

check.q: How did Rhys Davids and early translators render dukkha?
check.why: Early translators used 'suffering' or 'pain'.

check.q: Why did some later translators choose 'unsatisfactoriness'?
choices: Dukkha includes the sense that changing things never fully satisfy
check.why: They wanted to show dukkha's wider meaning.

check.q: What is connotation?
choices: The feelings a word suggests beyond its basic meaning
check.why: Word choice changes the reader's feeling.

lessons.title: Old English, New English
lessons.mainIdea: Victorian translations used formal, Bible-like English, which shaped how early readers imagined the Buddha.
reading: Many early translators used a formal English that echoed the King James Bible, with words like 'thee', 'verily' and 'brethren'. Readers heard the Buddha speaking like a biblical prophet.

Some key words were translated with Christian terms. 'Sin', 'heaven' and 'priest' sometimes appeared where the Pali meant something different. Scholars call this *domestication*: making a foreign text sound familiar.

Modern translators often use plainer English and keep Pali terms like dukkha, nibbana and kamma with explanations. Each approach has costs and gains, and comparing translations helps a reader spot a translator's *choices*.

words.d: making a foreign text sound familiar to readers, sometimes changing its meaning
decisions a translator makes about words and style

look.title: Victorian Voice
look.text: In Rhys Davids' 1881 English, the first sermon addresses the monks as 'brethren' and describes a 'noble truth concerning suffering', in a formal style much like the English Bible.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11); tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881)
look.prompt: How might a Christian reader in 1881 have heard this style?

check.q: What English did many Victorian translators echo?
check.why: They used formal, Bible-like language.

check.q: What is domestication in translation?
choices: Making a foreign text sound familiar, sometimes changing its meaning
check.why: Using terms like 'sin' domesticated Buddhist ideas.

check.q: What do many modern translators do with key Pali terms?
check.why: Keeping terms like dukkha avoids misleading matches.

lessons.title: Who Speaks for Buddhism?
lessons.mainIdea: Western scholars and Asian Buddhists shaped the modern picture of Buddhism together, and sometimes disagreed.
reading: Some Western scholars in the 1800s thought the 'real' Buddhism was found in ancient texts, not in the temples, rituals and relics they saw in Asia. They sometimes judged living Buddhists as having strayed from the texts.
Asian Buddhists pushed back and shaped the picture too. Monks in Sri Lanka and Burma taught the scholars. Leaders like Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku chose how to present their traditions abroad.

Scholars today describe Buddhism as both texts and living *practice*, from chanting and offerings to festivals and meditation. They ask whose *representation* of a tradition is being given, and they include the voices of practitioners.

words.d: how a person or group is described or shown to others
what religious people actually do, such as rituals and festivals

look.title: Two Pictures of Buddhism
look.text: A Victorian scholar writes: true Buddhism is found in the Pali texts, a philosophy of reason. A Sri Lankan grandmother says: Buddhism is going to the temple on Poya day, offering flowers, hearing the monks chant and keeping the precepts.
look.prompt: What does each picture include? What does each leave out?

check.q: Where did some 1800s Western scholars think 'real' Buddhism was found?
check.why: They privileged texts over living practice.

check.q: How did Asian Buddhists shape the modern picture?
choices: By teaching scholars and presenting their own traditions
check.why: Monks taught scholars and leaders spoke abroad.

check.q: What is representation?
choices: How a group is described to others
check.why: Scholars ask who represents a tradition and how.
